data.name: eIF4E
data.description: Cap-binding protein that recruits the ribosome to an mRNA. Held hostage by 4E-BP1 until mTORC1 phosphorylates the latter - the rate-limiting step of cap-dependent translation.
data.description_beginner: A protein that grabs onto mRNA and starts the process of building a new protein from it. Normally it's held back by 4E-BP1; mTORC1 releases that hold, which is the key step that turns on protein production.

reading_levels.beginner: The clamp that starts reading mRNA.
reading_levels.research: Rate-limiting for cap-dependent initiation; a proto-oncogene in its own right when overexpressed.

studies.title: A unifying model for mTORC1-mediated regulation of mRNA translation
studies.authors: Thoreen CC; Chantranupong L; Keys HR; Wang T; Gray NS; Sabatini DM

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Used ribosome profiling with the complete inhibitor Torin1 to address a long-standing debate: in these cells, mTORC1's translational control runs largely through the 4E-BP family acting on a specific class of mRNAs (TOP motifs). Losing just the 4E-BPs makes translation of TOP mRNAs resistant to mTOR inhibition - naming them the master effectors.

studies.title: The translational landscape of mTOR signalling steers cancer initiation and metastasis
studies.authors: Hsieh AC; Liu Yi; Edlind MP; Ingolia NT; Janes MR; Sher A; Shi EY; Stumpf CR; Christensen C; Bonham MJ; Wang S; Ren P; Martin M; Jessen K; Feldman ME; Weissman JS; Shokat KM; Rommel C; Ruggero D

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Showed WHY mTOR-driven translation matters for cancer: in prostate cancer, oncogenic mTOR selectively translates a specific set of pro-invasion mRNAs that drive metastasis. An ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor (INK128) reversed that signature - an early preclinical rationale from mouse models and cell lines, not a clinical result.

studies.title: Tuberous sclerosis complex-1 and -2 gene products function together to inhibit mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR)-mediated downstream signaling
studies.authors: Tee AR; Fingar DC; Manning BD; Kwiatkowski DJ; Cantley LC; Blenis J

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Cultured mammalian cells (HEK293-type transfection system per MeSH 'Cell Line'); coexpression of TSC1/TSC2, patient-derived TSC2 mutant, rapamycin-resistant S6K1 mutants
studies.finding: The authors coexpressed hamartin (TSC1) and tuberin (TSC2) in cultured cells and followed two main outputs of mTOR. Together, the two proteins reduced phosphorylation of 4E-BP1, so more 4E-BP1 stayed bound to the translation factor eIF4E; a TSC2 mutant found in TSC patients was defective at this. Hamartin plus tuberin also lowered S6K1 activity, but did not affect S6K1 mutants that resist rapamycin, which points to mTOR as the step being blocked. In nutrient-deprived cells, hamartin and tuberin prevented amino acids from switching S6K1 back on. The authors concluded that the TSC1-TSC2 complex acts as an inhibitor of mTOR signalling and suggested that TSC tumours may come from too much mTOR activity. Boundary: overexpression in cultured mammalian cells; the link to tumours in TSC patients is a proposal, not tested in patient tissue here.

studies.title: Translational control of long-lasting synaptic plasticity and memory
studies.authors: Costa-Mattioli M; Sossin WS; Klann E; Sonenberg N

evidence.label: Review — secondary literature, not a new result
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Narrative review (no new data): genetic, physiological, pharmacological and biochemical studies in rodents, Aplysia and Drosophila
studies.finding: This review gathers evidence that long-lasting synaptic plasticity and long-term memory depend on new protein synthesis, and that the step where mRNA translation starts is a main control point. It covers two arms: the mTORC1 arm (4E-BP2, eIF4E, S6K) that controls cap-dependent translation, and the eIF2alpha arm (GCN2, PKR, ATF4) that controls general translation and specific mRNAs. It also discusses how faulty translational control is linked to disorders such as fragile X syndrome and tuberous sclerosis. It is a summary of work by many labs and gives the field a shared framework rather than new data. Boundary: narrative review; the cited evidence is mainly from rodent slices, rodent behaviour and invertebrate models, not from people.

studies.title: A rapamycin-sensitive signaling pathway contributes to long-term synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus
studies.authors: Tang SJ; Reis G; Kang H; Gingras AC; Sonenberg N; Schuman EM

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Rat and mouse hippocampal slices (field recordings, immunostaining); cultured rat hippocampal neurons; Western blot of rat hippocampus
studies.finding: The authors showed that mTOR, 4E-BP1, 4E-BP2 and eIF4E are present in rat hippocampus and sit in dendrites, close to synapses, where their staining overlapped with the postsynaptic protein PSD-95. Blocking mTOR with rapamycin in hippocampal slices reduced late-phase long-term potentiation (LTP) after high-frequency stimulation, while early-phase LTP was unaffected. Rapamycin also blocked the synaptic potentiation induced by the growth factor BDNF. This was one of the early papers to tie a rapamycin-sensitive pathway to the protein-synthesis-dependent phase of synaptic plasticity and to suggest it controls local translation at synapses. Boundary: rodent brain slices and cultured neurons; mTOR targets were localised but their phosphorylation during LTP was not reported in the abstract; no behaviour or memory test.

studies.title: Autism-related deficits via dysregulated eIF4E-dependent translational control
studies.authors: Gkogkas CG; Khoutorsky A; Ran I; Rampakakis E; Nevarko T; Weatherill DB; Vasuta C; Yee S; Truitt M; Dallaire P; Major F; Lasko P; Ruggero D; Nader K; Lacaille JC; Sonenberg N

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Eif4ebp2 knockout mice and betaT-Eif4e (eIF4E-overexpressing) mice; hippocampal slices and slice cultures; MEF reporter assays; icv 4EGI-1 and lentiviral shRNA
studies.finding: Mice lacking 4E-BP2, the main brain brake on eIF4E downstream of mTORC1, showed autism-like behaviours: reduced social approach in the three-chamber test, more self-grooming and marble burying, and more ultrasonic calls as pups. Polysome profiling of hippocampus showed that, of 24 autism-linked mRNAs tested, only the neuroligin 1-4 mRNAs shifted to heavier polysomes in the knockout, with no change in their mRNA levels or in global protein synthesis; eIF4E-overexpressing mice showed the same neuroligin shift. Knockout neurons had larger excitatory than inhibitory synaptic charge transfer, raising the excitation/inhibition ratio. Five days of brain infusion of 4EGI-1, which blocks eIF4E binding to eIF4G, brought cap-bound eIF4E/eIF4G and neuroligin levels back to normal and reversed the social deficit, and knocking down neuroligin 1 (but not neuroligin 2) partly restored social behaviour. Boundary: mouse genetic models (male mice for behaviour); mTOR itself was not manipulated; the link to human autism is by analogy.

relations.mechanism: Unphosphorylated 4E-BP1 clamps onto eIF4E and stops it assembling the cap-binding complex. mTORC1 phosphorylates 4E-BP1 to release that grip - so the brake on translation is released, not the accelerator pressed.
relations.mechanism_beginner: Untagged 4E-BP1 clamps onto eIF4E and blocks it; mTORC1 tags 4E-BP1 to make it let go – releasing a brake, not pressing an accelerator.
relations.boundary: Biochemical and cell-culture evidence (in vitro assays, mammalian and mouse cells, plus one review). It establishes the binding switch itself. It does not measure how much translation changes in a given tissue, in whole animals or in people.

relations.mechanism: Free eIF4E recruits the ribosome to the mRNA cap. This is the step that actually turns a growth signal into new protein.
relations.mechanism_beginner: Freed eIF4E brings the ribosome to the mRNA – the step that actually turns a growth signal into new protein.
relations.boundary: Biochemical and cell-based evidence (mouse cells with ribosome profiling, mouse models with human prostate cancer data in one study) plus a review. How much a given tissue depends on eIF4E-driven translation is not settled by these sources.
relations.note: Not every mRNA is equally sensitive - HSI2012 shows a specific translational program, not a uniform increase.
